n: While others go home, Jesus goes out to the Mount of Olives, east of Jerusalem across the Kidron Valley, where he often spent the night during visits to the city.
At dawn he is back in the temple courts. People gather, and he sits down to teach them, as rabbis did.

f.w: he sat down, and taught them

n: Religious leaders interrupt, dragging in a woman caught in adultery and making her stand in front of everyone — a public humiliation.

f.g: Experts who copied, studied, and interpreted the law of Moses.

n: They address Jesus as “Master” (teacher) and stress she was caught in the act. Pointedly, the man involved is nowhere to be seen.

f.g: The law required that both the man and the woman be punished.

n: They cite the law of Moses that such people be stoned and demand Jesus’s ruling.
It is a trap: if he says to spare her, he contradicts Moses; if he says to stone her, he loses his reputation for mercy and defies Roman rule. Jesus quietly stoops and writes in the dust.

f.g: tempting = testing, trying to trap.
John doesn’t say what he wrote; many have guessed, but the text leaves it unknown.

n: When they keep pressing, Jesus stands and says: let the one without sin throw the first stone. He upholds the law while turning their judgment back on their own hearts.

f.w: He that is without sin among you
f.g: Under the law, the witnesses were to throw the first stones.

n: Then he bends down and writes on the ground again, giving them time to think.

f.g: Some see an echo of Jeremiah: those who forsake the Lord “shall be written in the earth.”

n: Their consciences pierced, the accusers slip away one by one, oldest first, until only Jesus and the woman are left.

f.g: Perhaps the older men, with more life experience, recognized their own sins first.

n: Jesus stands and speaks to her gently, calling her “Woman” — a respectful form of address — and asks where her accusers have gone.

f.g: A polite term in that culture, not cold or rude.

n: She answers that no one has condemned her. Jesus, the only sinless one present, does not condemn her either — but he calls her to leave her sin behind. Mercy and the call to change come together.

f.w: Neither do I condemn thee: go, and sin no more
f.g: The JST adds: “And the woman glorified God from that hour, and believed on his name.”

n: Jesus declares, “I am the light of the world.” During this feast huge lamps were lit in the temple court; Jesus claims to be the true light that guides people out of darkness.

f.w: I am the light of the world

n: The Pharisees object that a man’s testimony about himself proves nothing legally.
Jesus replies that his testimony is still valid because he knows where he came from and where he is going — something they don’t know.

f.w: whence I came, and whither I go
f.g: whence = from where; whither = to where.

n: They judge by outward, human standards; Jesus did not come at this time to condemn anyone.

f.g: By merely human, worldly standards.

n: And when he does judge, his judgment is true, because he doesn’t judge alone — the Father who sent him is with him.
He points to their own law, which requires two witnesses to establish a matter.

f.w: the testimony of two men is true

n: He meets that standard: he is one witness, and his Father is the second. The Father and the Son are separate witnesses in perfect agreement.

f.w: the Father that sent me beareth witness of me

n: They ask where his Father is, thinking of an earthly father. Jesus answers that they know neither him nor the Father; to know Jesus is to know the Father.

f.w: ye should have known my Father also

n: John notes the location — the treasury area of the temple, near the offering chests in the Court of the Women. Still no one arrests him, because his hour hasn’t come.

f.g: Thirteen trumpet-shaped offering chests stood in the Court of the Women.

f.w: his hour was not yet come

n: Jesus warns again that he is going away. Those who reject him will die still burdened by their sins and cannot follow him to God.
His enemies mockingly wonder if he plans to kill himself, misreading his words about going where they can’t come.

f.g: A cruel joke; John’s readers know he will lay down his life, not take it (John 10:18).

n: Jesus contrasts their origin with his: they belong to this fallen world; he comes from above, from heaven.
That’s why they will die in their sins unless they believe that “I am he.” In Greek Jesus simply says “I am,” echoing God’s name revealed to Moses.

f.g: The word “he” is supplied by the translators; Jesus says egō eimi, “I am.”

n: “Who are you?” they demand. Jesus replies that he is exactly who he has told them from the start.
He could say much in judgment of them, but he speaks only what he has heard from his truthful Father.

f.w: those things which I have heard of him

n: John notes that they still didn’t realize he was talking about God the Father.
When they “lift up” the Son of Man — on the cross — they will recognize that he is the “I am,” acting only as the Father taught him.

f.w: lifted up the Son of man

n: The Father has not left him alone, because Jesus always does what pleases him. Perfect obedience means constant companionship with God.

f.w: I do always those things that please him

n: Even amid the conflict, many people put their faith in him as he speaks.
To these new believers Jesus explains true discipleship: it means continuing — staying, living — in his word, not just a moment of enthusiasm.

f.w: If ye continue in my word

n: They will come to know the truth, and that truth will set them free — from sin, error, and fear.

f.w: the truth shall make you free

n: Offended, some answer that as Abraham’s descendants they have never been slaves to anyone — a bold claim given Egypt, Babylon, and the Roman occupation.
Jesus explains the bondage he means: anyone who commits sin becomes its slave.

f.g: servant = slave (Greek doulos).

n: A slave has no permanent place in a household, but a son belongs there forever.
So if the Son sets them free, they will be truly free. Real freedom comes through Christ.
Yes, they are Abraham’s physical descendants — but they want to kill him because his word has found no room in their hearts.

f.w: my word hath no place in you

n: Jesus speaks what he has seen with his Father; they act on what they have learned from their “father” — a hint he will make plain in verse 44.

f.g: Jesus is speaking of spiritual parentage — whose example they follow.

n: They insist Abraham is their father. Jesus replies that true children of Abraham would act like Abraham — in faith and obedience.
Abraham welcomed God’s messengers; he never tried to kill someone who spoke God’s truth.
They retort that they are not illegitimate — perhaps a sly jab at the rumors about Jesus’s birth — and claim God alone as their Father.

f.w: We be not born of fornication
f.g: Possibly an insult implying doubts about Jesus’s own birth.

n: If God were truly their Father, they would love Jesus, because he came from God and was sent by him.

f.w: I proceeded forth and came from God

n: They can’t understand his words because they are unwilling to really hear them.
In his strongest rebuke, Jesus says their true father is the devil, whose desires they carry out. Satan has been a murderer and a liar from the beginning.
Because Jesus tells them the truth, they refuse to believe him — the opposite of what should happen.
Jesus challenges anyone to prove him guilty of a single sin. No one can. So why not believe the truth he speaks?

f.w: Which of you convinceth me of sin?
f.g: convinceth = convicts, proves guilty.

n: Those who belong to God listen to God’s words. Their refusal to listen shows where they really stand.

f.w: He that is of God heareth God's words

n: They hurl insults: he is a Samaritan — a despised outsider — and possessed by a demon.

f.g: Jews and Samaritans had centuries of hostility over religion and ancestry.

n: Jesus calmly denies the charge. He honors his Father, while they dishonor him.
He isn’t seeking glory for himself; God the Father seeks his honor and will be the judge.

f.w: I seek not mine own glory

n: Then a great promise: anyone who keeps his word will never experience death — meaning spiritual death, separation from God.
His opponents take it literally: Abraham and the prophets died, so how can Jesus promise no one will taste death?

f.g: An idiom for experiencing death.

n: “Are you greater than Abraham?” they ask. Who does he think he is? The answer, as John’s readers know, is yes.
Jesus replies that self-praise would be worthless; it is his Father — the God they claim — who honors him.

f.w: it is my Father that honoureth me

n: They don’t really know God, but he does. To deny that would make him a liar; he knows the Father and keeps his word.

f.w: I know him, and keep his saying

n: Jesus says Abraham rejoiced to see his day — he saw it and was glad. Latter-day scripture confirms that Abraham and other ancient prophets saw and knew of Christ.

f.w: Abraham rejoiced to see my day

n: They scoff: he isn’t even fifty years old, yet claims to have seen Abraham, who lived some two thousand years before?

f.g: A round number meaning “you’re still a young man”; Jesus was probably in his early thirties.

n: Jesus makes his boldest claim: before Abraham was born, “I am.” He identifies himself as the eternal God who spoke to Moses — Jehovah, the premortal Christ.

f.g: Latter-day Saints understand Jesus Christ to be Jehovah, the God of the Old Testament.

n: Understanding the claim, they grab stones to execute him for blasphemy. But Jesus slips away through the crowd and leaves the temple — his hour still had not come.

f.w: going through the midst of them
